mstts:express-as.prosody: Welcome—I'm so glad you're joining me for this journey. You know, there are moments in everyday life—quick glances, offhand comments, or even the silence in a room—that can carry so much more than we realize. Together, we'll explore those subtle, sometimes invisible lines where the personal and the collective meet, and how they shape not just how we see the world, but also how we see ourselves. In Citizen: An American Lyric, Claudia Rankine invites us to move through these experiences side by side. Through her poetic storytelling, she shows us how microaggressions, history, and the weight of everyday encounters can change what it means to belong—and what it means to be seen or unseen. As we walk through her vignettes and reflections, we'll get a sense of how language, silence, and even a simple gesture can lift us up or cut us deeply. We’ll also see how the realities of Black life in America are lived, felt, and endured—with both vulnerability and incredible resilience. So, let’s open ourselves to these stories and insights, and discover together how the meaning of citizenship, dignity, and visibility is woven into the fabric of the American experience. I hope you’re ready, because there’s so much here to reflect on, to feel, and to carry forward with us.

Chapter 1. Everyday Encounters That Shape a Sense of Belonging.
You know, it often starts with the tiniest things—a passing comment, a quick look, maybe even a question that seems innocent, but somehow, it stings. Most people barely notice these moments. But if you’re on the receiving end, they start to stack up, shaping the way you move through the world.
Picture this: your day begins at the coffee shop. The greeting is simple, but then, the barista hesitates. Their eyes flicker. Suddenly, you feel your presence being measured, weighed, maybe even quietly questioned.
These things don’t just happen in one place. In classrooms, offices, even just walking down the street, there’s this constant back and forth—almost like a negotiation. Imagine a woman sitting in a meeting, sharing her idea… only to have it ignored until someone else repeats it. Or a man shopping, feeling the security guard’s gaze linger just a bit too long. Or maybe a child in class, being asked, “Where are you really from?” It sounds casual, but the message underneath is clear: you don’t quite fit in.
These moments aren’t usually loud or explosive. Most of the time, they’re quiet—almost invisible to folks who don’t experience them. But for those who do, the impact builds up. Each little moment becomes a small weight, pressing down, reminding you of boundaries that other people set. And over time, all those weights shape not just how you’re seen, but how you start to see yourself.
There’s a special kind of exhaustion that comes with deciding, again and again, whether to speak up or just let it slide. Should the woman in the meeting call it out and risk being labeled “difficult?” Should the man in the store confront the guard, or just keep moving? Most days, it seems easier to stay quiet, to swallow that discomfort and carry on. But staying silent comes with a cost. It settles in your body, a tension that never fully goes away.
In the middle of all these daily negotiations, there’s often a longing—a wish for things to be easy, for the simple comfort of not having to explain or defend who you are. And sometimes, that wish is met with disappointment. Even among friends, there are misunderstandings. A joke lands wrong, a story gets brushed off, and suddenly, the gap between people feels huge.
Still, every so often, there are moments of real connection. Maybe it’s a friend who sees your discomfort and quietly offers their support. Or a stranger who catches your eye and gives you a genuine smile, recognizing your shared humanity. These moments don’t erase the pain, but they do offer a bit of relief—a reminder that belonging is possible, even if it never feels permanent.
As the day winds down, those memories linger. Some replay in your mind, the words echoing long after. Others, you push aside because they’re just too heavy. But no matter what, they leave their mark. They shape your day, and over time, your sense of self.
That’s how the ordinary becomes something extraordinary—a living record of what it means to move through the world in a body that’s always being watched, always being questioned.

Chapter Two: The Weight of Words and the Power of Silence.
You know, language really is a powerful thing. It’s a tool we all use every day, but sometimes, it turns into a weapon without us even realizing it. Think about it—how often do words just slip out, maybe in the middle of a chat with a coworker or during a quick conversation with a neighbor? Sometimes those words are meant to be harmless, but their impact can run deep. Picture a colleague tossing out a comment about “articulate” speech, totally unaware of what that might imply. Or maybe a neighbor cracks a joke about someone’s hair, not knowing the history or the pain tied to that topic. Those words stick with you. They echo in your head long after the conversation’s over. And if you’re on the receiving end, there’s this constant calculation going on in your mind. Should you say something? Will it even matter if you do? Most of the time, it just feels easier to let it go. The idea of having to explain or educate someone—it’s exhausting. So, you end up carrying those words, adding them to a growing pile of small hurts and misunderstandings. But here’s something to pay attention to—silence isn’t always a choice. Sometimes, it’s what you need to keep yourself safe. Imagine a student in class, listening as a teacher mispronounces their name. They want to correct them, but they stay quiet. Or think about an employee at work, laughing along with a joke that actually stings, just so they’re not labeled as “too sensitive.” That kind of silence is heavy. It protects you, but it can also weigh you down. Every now and then, though, that silence breaks. Maybe a friend finally decides to speak up, naming the hurt that’s been building up inside. Yeah, the conversation feels awkward—maybe even painful—but it’s also important. In those moments, there’s this huge sense of relief. Sure, the words might not come out perfectly, but at least they’re honest. And it’s not all negative. Sometimes, language is what brings us together. Sharing stories in private, whispering the things that are hard to say out loud—that’s how we start to heal. There’s this quiet understanding in those conversations, a kind of gentle reminder that, yes, the pain is real, but you’re not alone in it. Still, we can't ignore that language cuts both ways. It can open up, but it can also hide things away. In public, people often steer clear of talking about race. It’s too uncomfortable, too likely to cause a stir. But that kind of silence? It’s deafening. It’s like refusing to see the truth that so many people live with every single day.

Chapter 3: The Body as a Site of Public Scrutiny and Private Pain
Let’s talk about what it really feels like to move through the world in a body that others see as different. It’s not just something out there—it’s both public and deeply personal, all at once.
Picture this: you’re out for a jog, and you feel those eyes following you. Or you step into an upscale boutique, and suddenly, you can just sense suspicion hanging in the air. Even in places that should feel safe, your body can become a battleground of tension and awareness.
Now, here’s something to pay attention to—not all of this scrutiny comes from the outside. Over time, it creeps in. You start to anticipate the looks, the questions, the judgments. Shoulders tense up, your posture shifts, every movement gets a little more careful. It’s almost like you’re performing—trying to blend in, aiming to seem non-threatening, hoping not to stand out. But no matter what you do, it feels like you can’t really escape notice.
Sometimes, that scrutiny turns harsh—even hostile. Maybe you’re pulled over while driving, and the situation escalates for no clear reason. Or you’re a teenager, just shopping, but suddenly you’re being followed and accused of theft with zero evidence. These moments aren’t just rare exceptions—they’re part of a bigger pattern. A constant reminder that, for some, the body always feels exposed, always at risk.
All this takes a real toll on the mind and spirit. Anxiety settles in, humming quietly in the background of every day. Sleep gets restless, dreams turn uneasy. Even if you try to move forward, your body keeps carrying the weight of these experiences.
But here’s the other side—your body isn’t just a target. It’s also a source of joy and strength. Think about those moments when you’re laughing with friends or dancing at a party. In those times, you feel free, unburdened. These flashes of happiness are precious, a reminder that your body is so much more than a site of pain—it’s also about pleasure and connection.
Still, the line between public and private is thin. The pain from public moments seeps into private ones, shaping how you see yourself and how you relate to others. Maybe a parent’s worried about their child’s safety, teaching them how to move through a world that isn’t always gentle. Or a partner offers comfort, but that underlying fear just won’t let go.
And then there’s the way art and media shape this whole dynamic. Images of violence against Black bodies get shared over and over, often stripped of context or care. Some folks get desensitized, while others are retraumatized, again and again. The body becomes a symbol, even a spectacle—its real humanity gets lost in a story about threat and danger.
So, what do we do in the face of all this? There’s a deep need to reclaim the body—to say, “Yes, I belong. I’m valuable. I have the right to exist without fear.” That act of reclamation? It’s resistance. It’s refusing to let others define your worth.
And maybe the most powerful thing to remember is this: despite everything, the body endures.

Chapter 4: Media, Violence, and the Shaping of Collective Memory
You know, the stories we see on the news, and the images that spread across our feeds, they don’t just inform us—they shape how we see ourselves and each other.
When violence erupts—let’s say a young man is shot by police, or a woman faces harassment on the street—suddenly, every detail gets picked apart and argued over. The victim’s entire life is put under a microscope, their choices questioned, and sometimes, their very humanity seems to be on trial.
For people who share the victim’s identity, these moments hit close to home. They aren’t just stories on a screen—they’re deeply personal. Each new report feels like a warning, a reminder that danger is never far away. And when these stories repeat, over and over, it starts to feel like violence isn’t just a possibility, but almost something you expect.
The role of the media in all this is... well, complicated. On one side, it shines a light on injustice, forcing us all to face tough realities we might rather ignore. But at the same time, it can turn real lives into mere headlines—stories that get boiled down to the most shocking details, rather than the full, complicated truth.
Too often, the focus sits on the spectacle, not the human being at the center of it all.
After violence strikes, there’s a sense of shared mourning. Communities come together—holding vigils, leading protests, raising their voices for justice. There’s pain, but also a fierce determination to be recognized and heard. These moments of unity are powerful. But let’s be honest—they’re also exhausting. It can feel like the cycle of violence and response just never stops, each new tragedy reopening the wounds from before.
That’s where art comes in. Through poetry, music, painting—people find ways to express what words alone can’t reach. These creative acts are more than just outlets for grief. They become forms of resistance—a way of saying, “We’re still here, and you won’t erase us.”
In the end, our collective memory is shaped by all these stories and images. For some, they become a rallying cry—a reason to stand up and push for change. For others, they’re a heavy weight, feeding fear or even despair.
The real challenge? It’s holding onto hope, and believing that a better future is within reach—even when the evidence sometimes says otherwise.

Let’s talk about something that’s both simple and complicated—friendship.
Chapter 5: Navigating Friendship, Trust, and the Limits of Empathy.
Friendships are shaped by the world around us, aren’t they?
No matter how close two people are—how much laughter, history, or trust they share—real life has a way of testing those bonds, especially when race and difference come into play.
Maybe you’ve been there: a friend lets something slip—a thoughtless joke, a tone-deaf comment. They don’t realize it stings, but you feel it. You pause, unsure. Do you say something? Or do you let it slide, telling yourself it’s not worth the trouble?
In moments like these, trust can feel so fragile. There’s this worry, right? That if you speak up, you’ll be labeled sensitive or confrontational. So, sometimes, silence seems easier. But that silence? It builds a wall. Suddenly, you’re a little more alone, even when you’re together.
Empathy is a beautiful thing, but let’s be honest—it has its limits. A friend may want to understand. They may listen, try to support you. But some things can’t be fully shared unless you’ve lived them. The sting of being left out, the constant need to watch what you say or do… how do you really explain that? It can be exhausting, for both sides.
But here’s the thing—sometimes, something shifts. A friend really listens. The conversation changes. For a moment, you don’t have to spell everything out. The pain is simply acknowledged. And just like that, the burden feels lighter. Those moments? They’re rare, but they’re real treasures. They remind us of what empathy can look like when it’s not just a word, but something we practice.
Of course, empathy has boundaries. Good intentions aren’t always enough. Understanding another person deeply takes time, humility, and the courage to sit with discomfort. It’s not easy. But it’s worth the effort.
So, next time you’re in one of those tough moments with a friend, remember—real connection is possible, even if it takes work.

Chapter 6. Bearing Witness: The Role of Art and the Artist.
Sometimes, the world’s pain just feels too big to carry all by yourself, doesn’t it? That’s where art steps in. It becomes this vessel—something that can hold what words alone just can’t seem to capture. And the artist, whether they’re working with a pen, a brush, or their voice, takes on the role of a witness. Not just for their own journey, but for the shared ache that weaves through families, neighborhoods, and entire communities.
Picture this: someone sits quietly at a desk, staring at a blank page. There’s this urge to create, but it’s tangled up with the heavy responsibility of telling the truth. How do you show what’s real without turning someone’s suffering into a spectacle? How do you honor the lives behind the headlines we scroll past every day? The artist’s hand might even tremble—not out of fear, but from knowing that every mark, every word, really matters.
You see art everywhere—sometimes it’s bold and loud, and sometimes you almost miss it. Maybe it’s a mural blooming across a city wall, faces painted in bright colors and deep shadows. People stop and look—some are moved, some get uncomfortable. For just a moment, the city’s busy rhythm slows down. That mural doesn’t erase the pain, but it demands to be seen. It quietly insists: this happened. We were here.
But art isn’t always some grand gesture. Sometimes it’s a poem scribbled at the edge of a notebook, a song hummed softly under someone’s breath, or a photograph carefully tucked into a wallet. These small acts of creation? They’re acts of survival. They help us process what’s happened, remember what matters, and push back against the silence that often follows trauma.
When you come across art like this, you have a choice. Some folks turn away, maybe because it stirs up something uncomfortable. Others linger, letting the work open a door inside them. In those moments, art turns into a bridge—a way to connect, to feel the heartbeat of someone else’s life.
But let’s be real: bearing witness takes a toll. The artist absorbs the pain they show us, carrying it in their body and mind. There’s always the risk of being overwhelmed, of getting lost in stories that aren’t their own. Yet, most artists keep going. They’re driven by this deep belief that telling the truth is worth it. That bearing witness is about honoring both the living and those we’ve lost.
Over time, all this art builds up. It becomes a record—a testament to how we endure, and how hope can take root even in hard places. It reminds us, as we see it, that we’re not alone. Our pain and joy—well, they’re part of something bigger. In this way, art doesn’t just mirror the world back to us. It shapes it, offering new ways to see, to feel, and to imagine what’s possible.

Chapter Seven: Microaggressions and the Unseen Labor of Survival.
There’s a kind of work that rarely gets noticed—a steady, almost invisible effort that goes into getting through a world that’s not always kind or welcoming. You won’t find this work on a resume, and it doesn’t show up in a paycheck. But you can feel its weight. It’s the work of always being ready—anticipating a comment, preparing an explanation, deciding if this is the moment to speak up, or if it’s safer to let it slide.
Imagine you’re on your morning commute. The train is packed, and you can sense the tension creeping into your shoulders. Someone’s stare lingers just a little too long. There’s an empty seat, but no one takes it, even as the car gets more crowded. And you can’t help but wonder— is it something about me? That question—quiet but persistent—never really goes away, does it?
Then, at work, it continues. Maybe a colleague cracks a joke that just doesn’t sit right. Laughter circles the room, and you find yourself smiling along, even though your stomach tightens. Later, maybe in the bathroom, you replay what happened and ask yourself, “Should I have said something?” There’s always this mental math—will speaking up help, or will it just make things harder?
And it’s not just at work. It follows you into stores, onto sidewalks, into classrooms. There’s this ongoing need to manage how others see you, to always be a little bit on guard, ready to defend your place. Most people don’t notice this constant vigilance, but for those who live it, the cost is real. It can show up as exhaustion, irritability, or just feeling stretched so thin you might snap.
Sometimes, though, this unseen labor is shared. Friends get together and trade stories—comparing notes on the day’s microaggressions. There’s comfort in knowing someone else gets it, but also this frustration: why should we have to do this work at all? These conversations are a mix of laughter and sighs—a way to get by, even if they don’t fix the problem.
Over time, all those little moments can pile up. Your body absorbs the stress, and your mind gets tired. Still, most people keep going—finding small ways to recharge. Maybe it’s a walk outside, playing your favorite song, or just a quiet night at home. These little rituals become acts of self-preservation.
The hope is that by naming this invisible labor, we can start to change it. Maybe, just maybe, people who never noticed before will begin to see it—and the weight can be shared a little more fairly. But until that day comes, the work continues. Quiet, invisible, and absolutely essential.

Chapter 8: The Struggle for Recognition and the Politics of Visibility
Recognition really is one of our most basic needs. It’s that deep desire to be seen, to be acknowledged, to have your reality affirmed by others. But for so many people, recognition isn’t easy. It’s often hard-won, always a little incomplete, and sometimes it feels like it could vanish at any moment.
Think about this: the struggle to be visible isn’t just about catching someone’s attention. It’s about being understood, and being understood on your own terms.
Picture this memory for a moment. There’s a student in class, hand raised, eager to say something. But the teacher calls on someone else. That student’s hand drops, and the moment slips by... but the feeling? That sticks around. It’s not simply about being overlooked—it’s about feeling invisible.
Out in the world, the politics of visibility play out on a much bigger stage. Imagine the streets filled with protestors, their voices rising together, demanding to be heard. The media shows up, cameras rolling, but the story that gets told? Sometimes it’s not the story those protestors wanted to share. Their message is filtered, maybe even distorted.
Here’s the risk—visibility can end up being just another way people are erased. It becomes a spectacle, something that actually hides the real issues underneath.
On a personal level, the need for recognition is rarely simple. There’s a kind of pride in being seen, but also a real fear. When you’re visible, you’re open to scrutiny, and that can bring backlash. Some people decide it’s safer to keep their heads down, to avoid the spotlight. But others? They step right into it, determined to claim their space, no matter what it costs.
Even in families and close communities, this struggle shows up in all kinds of ways. A parent tries to share their experience with their child, searching for the right words that might make sense. A friend listens, nods along, but just doesn’t quite get it. That gap—the space between being seen and being truly known—can feel huge.
And yet, there are those rare, powerful moments when recognition is real. Maybe a teacher finally hears a student’s voice. Or a protester’s words reach someone who really needed to hear them. Or a friend simply says, “I see you,” and you know they mean it. These moments are rare, but they matter so much.
They give us a glimpse of what’s possible when we look past assumptions and really, honestly see each other.
The politics of visibility are complicated—shaped by power, by history, by who gets to decide what’s seen and what’s ignored. But this need for recognition? It never goes away. At the heart of every struggle, there’s that deep desire: to be seen—not as a symbol, but as a person.

Chapter 9: Collective Grief, Resilience, and the Search for Justice.
When tragedy hits, it isn’t just a personal loss—it’s something the whole community feels. Have you ever noticed how, when violence touches a neighborhood or a group, there’s this almost tangible heaviness in the air? People gather together, mourning side by side, their shared grief a powerful reminder of how deeply we're all connected. Even the lightest moments—like laughter—somehow seem tinged with sorrow.
But here’s the thing: in these hardest moments, resilience begins to shine through. Not because anyone is pretending the pain isn’t real, but because people simply refuse to be broken by it. You’ll see folks organizing candlelight vigils, planning marches, or coming together for memorials. Candles flicker in the darkness, names are spoken aloud, and tears fall—sometimes quietly, sometimes in front of everyone. These acts of mourning aren’t just about grief—they’re also acts of defiance, a way to say, “This life mattered. This story deserves to be heard.”
And yet, justice can feel so far away. Systems that are supposed to protect us sometimes fall short, leaving families and entire communities to pick up the pieces themselves. The search for answers, for accountability—it’s often a long, painful road, filled with setbacks and moments of real disappointment. Still, people keep moving forward. They’re driven by the memory of loved ones, by hope that real change is possible.
Picture this: a mother stands at a podium, her voice steady but her hands trembling. She says her child’s name for everyone to hear, making sure it’s never forgotten. The crowd is silent—some people are wiping away tears. In that moment, grief and hope live side by side. It’s a powerful reminder: fighting for justice is also about fighting to remember.
Resilience isn’t just about surviving; it’s about changing and growing. Communities find ways to heal together, to offer support, and to imagine something better. Art, music, storytelling—they become lifelines. They help people process their pain and start to dream of a future that looks different from the past.
The journey toward justice doesn’t have a neat ending. It’s ongoing—filled with heartbreak, but also with hope. Along the way, there are small victories: maybe a new law gets passed, a partnership forms, or someone’s story finally gets the recognition it deserves. These wins don’t erase the pain, but they do give people a sense of progress—a reason to keep going.

Let’s talk about Chapter 10: Imagining New Futures—Hope, Healing, and the Ongoing Work.
So, after everything we’ve explored—the stories, the pain, the struggle—there’s this lingering question: What now?
How do we move forward, holding onto all that’s happened, but still reaching for something better? You might guess the answer isn’t simple. But it all begins with imagination—with being bold enough to picture a world that’s different from the one we know today.
Hope isn’t some naïve wish. It’s hard-won, shaped by disappointment and loss. It lives in those tiny moments that break through even on the toughest days. Maybe it’s a neighbor checking in, or a stranger offering you a seat, or a child laughing freely. Those moments? They’re seeds, planted right in the soil of our everyday lives.
Healing isn’t a finish line we cross—it’s a journey. Sometimes it happens in therapy, sometimes in late-night talks with a friend, or maybe just during a quiet walk through the city. It’s slow, it’s uneven, and yeah, sometimes it hurts. But it is possible. Those scars will stick around, but they don’t have to shape your future.
The work of building a better world? It never really ends. It’s happening all the time—in classrooms, in courtrooms, right in our own living rooms. It takes courage. The courage to speak up, to really listen, and to be open to change. And let’s be honest—it takes humility too. We all mess up sometimes, and being willing to admit that, and learn from it, is just as important.
Picture this: a community where every person is seen and valued. Where our differences aren’t something to fear, but something that makes us stronger. That vision isn’t just wishful thinking. It’s a real possibility, shaped by the choices we make every single day. It’s built in those small moments of connection, in standing together, and in refusing to let injustice go unchallenged.
The journey? It’s long, and it’s not always easy. But here’s the hope: by bearing witness, by speaking the truth, and by never staying silent, we can create something new. A world where belonging isn’t a privilege—it’s just the way things are. Where justice isn’t only a dream, but something we actually live.

As we wrap up, let’s pause and really take in what this journey has shown us.
Those small, everyday moments? They matter more than we realize. They shape how we see ourselves, and how we feel we belong.
Even silence—or the words we choose—can carry so much weight. They mold our relationships, our memories, and even the stories we pass down.
Our bodies, too, carry their own stories. Sometimes they feel vulnerable, but they can also be powerful sources of strength and joy.
And let’s not forget the power of art and storytelling. They help us bear witness, connect, and remind each other that we’re not alone in this.
The fight for recognition and justice? It’s ongoing. But it’s fueled by resilience and hope—qualities you carry with you.
If you’ve come this far, you’ve walked through a landscape of stories—some painful, some full of hope, all deeply human.
The path we’ve traced through *Citizen: An American Lyric* isn’t just about facing wounds and exclusion. It’s about how we keep healing, how we keep imagining new ways to live together.
There aren’t always easy answers. But there is comfort in knowing you’re not alone—in your questions, your struggles, or your longing for a better world.
So, as you move forward, remember: real change begins in those tiny, everyday moments. In the words you say. The stories you listen to. The ways you show up for people around you.
Let yourself be unsettled—but let yourself be moved, too.
The work of justice and belonging, it never really ends. But every act of witness, every small gesture of care, brings us all a little closer to the world we’re hoping to build.
You’re a part of that story now. So, keep going.
